On the first interpretation, the argument proves that the world began, in the manner of theologians who treat the matter rather simply. On the second, it establishes God's power and freedom, as those theologians understand them.

There is a further distinction. On the first interpretation, the freedom included in God's power is possibility in practice: it is supposed to allow a period in time when the act and the agent are apart. On the second, it is possibility in itself: the act is considered as something whose nature does not make it necessary.

The author rejects both kinds of possibility when applied to God's bringing things into being. All that His power requires is the conditional statement already given. A conditional can be true even when both its parts are true, both false, one true and the other false, or when necessity and impossibility are involved. In this argument, the words introducing the condition concern the meanings of the statements, not separate events that must happen in time.
The note corrects the wording: the point is God's power or capacity to act.
Two problems arise if one says God must be able to will pure inaction: that would deny His role as the source of action, and the will cannot be directed to sheer nonexistence.
This argument defines God's power by a possibility that belongs to the created effect. The author says an attribute of God cannot be explained by a feature of what He creates.

If one will can select between equal options without a reason, the same question applies to that will: why this one rather than another? The answer either repeats without end or allows a choice for no reason. — س قده
If neither side is necessary, neither side is settled. The fact that one side occurs shows that a cause has made it necessary; without that, the effect remains possible. — س قده
Possibility here means that neither side is necessary, not that the two sides are equally likely. A preference that falls short of necessity does not end the effect's need for a cause. — س قده
A long chain of preferences still allows the opposite outcome, just as the first preference does. Unless every way for the effect not to happen is closed, it has not become necessary. — س قده
For the author, true existence must come from the necessary source. A mere possibility or preference cannot bring the “light” of actual existence by itself.
Human will is a strong desire that reaches the point of action. The action normally follows from it, and the will takes its particular identity from the thing it wills. — س قده
Will has no identity apart from what it is directed toward. The author also hints that will is a kind of knowing what is good and fitting.
God's unity is not the limited unity of one item among others. It is a real, all-encompassing unity that relates to every existing thing. — س قده
The will and what it wills come from one source, like existence and what exists. The note connects this to love: the higher loves what comes from it, while the lower is drawn toward the higher.
The author distinguishes the early Muʿtazilites from later theologians who say that an effect does not exist until its cause makes it necessary.
If a cause does not make its effect necessary, the result is no better than saying it happens by chance, whether there was no preference or only a weak one. — س قده
The word “or” suggests that the author meant to discuss al-Kaʿbī's view in more detail. That part may be missing from the source copy. — س قده
The author explains this saying in the lines that follow: it rules out a cause of God's essence, not a reason for a particular act.
Here “act” first means the thing created; then it means the act of creating. — س قده
The leading philosophers had also reached this account, as reports of their views in discussions of substances, in Keys to the Unseen, and in the author's Treatise on Coming into Being show.

The author's explanation rests on change in substance itself, a view that sets his approach apart among Muslim philosophers. It gives a strong account of both sides of the question: the natural world begins again and again and never stands still, while God's gift of existence never runs out and His words are never exhausted. To claim that the world began in a way that required God's generosity to cease is, in this account, a cure worse than the disease.

The author's teacher also defended a form of coming into being that is prior to ordinary time. This too is a serious view that tries to reconcile both truths. But the author's position, that the world begins in time, agrees more closely with the language of the revealed religions.

This is an explicit statement of the movement of substance itself. More generally, the teachers in question arrived at the view that the world continually comes into being through both direct spiritual insight and rational argument.

Direct insight is a familiar part of their practice. The words of Ibn Arabi, quoted earlier in the discussion of motion, and those of Rumi and other teachers make this plain. They did not build their beliefs merely on repeating what others said. Rumi writes:
From the Giver, the gift comes fresh, and fresh again; Yet in the body it seems to flow without a break.
There are many passages of this kind. Sanāʾī of Ghazna also writes:
Spiders turn flies into dried provisions; Those who know God celebrate two feasts in a breath.

The objection treats the possible thing's existence and nonexistence as though they were the same as God's ability to create or not create it. A thing may be possible in itself even when its existence necessarily follows from God's eternal act.
A thing's existence can be necessary through its cause while its essence remains possible in itself.

The necessity mentioned in the objection is necessity in itself. If the world's coming into existence were necessary in itself, there would be more than one being necessary in itself, which is impossible. Nor can this necessity simply be the necessity of God's own essence: the argument describes it as something understood in relation to another, whereas God's essence is not dependent on any such relation.

Perhaps the intended claim is that the world's existence is necessary through God's necessity. The author earlier distinguished this from a thing being made necessary by His action. Or perhaps it means necessity in relation to God: as God is necessary in Himself, He is necessary in relation to the world as a whole, and the first thing that comes from Him is necessary in relation to Him.

Another reply is to distinguish the two sides of coming into existence. In its relation of dependence on God, the world's existence is necessary, because the One whose existence is necessary lacks no perfection. Considered as the world's own existence, it is possible in itself. The same coming into existence can thus be necessary from the side of its cause and possible from the side of its effect.
This refers to Muḥammad al-Khafrī, who argued that power is the possibility of acting or not acting when we consider the agent in itself, while action becomes necessary when will is included.

The sound meaning of “a position between the two” is this: causing and bringing things into being depend on existence. Nothing acts before it exists. Every existence, whether of a cause or an effect, has a relation to God when considered apart from the separate essences to which we give names. In that respect, the effects of created existence are effects of God's existence. But existence also has a relation to the essences of created things; in that respect they have their own effects, just as they have their own existence.

If we look at existence in its necessary dependence on God, we speak of all things being under His power. This is the oneness of acts grounded in the oneness of His essence and attributes. It is not the fatalist's account, which speaks of the oneness of acts while leaving the oneness of God's reality unexplained. An effect points us back to its source.
If, instead, we look at existence as belonging to possible things, we speak of choice and action. A person who understands both sides does not erase either of them.

Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī's distinction between first and immediate causes can be read in this way. We could even reverse the description while keeping its point: seen as God's, existence displays the action of the one who freely wills; seen as belonging to creatures, it shows their dependence on a creator whose power rules over them. The first explanation is easier to grasp. The second makes a subtler distinction.
Created agents may look as if they choose, yet their choices are shaped by motives and causes beyond them. This is not choice in the same way as God's.
Power and will involve knowledge and awareness; they are not blind forces.
Created things follow from God necessarily, not merely as something that could happen or is more likely to happen. Necessity does not rule out power or choice. — س قده
God's knowledge is active: it brings about what He knows. In this sense, it is His will. — س قده
The order flows from God through a sequence of causes; this does not mean that all things come into being at once. — س قده
A result fits the nature of its cause. This fit is part of what it means for an agent to will its action. — س قده

The body’s nutritive power assimilates food into the living body, much as a fire changes what it consumes. The author quotes Rumi: “When bread joined the human body, dead bread became alive and aware.”

One thing can exist in different ways: knowledge may be an inner quality, a kind of substance in the soul or intellect, or God's necessary knowledge of Himself. “One essence” here means one shared idea, not one essence belonging to several categories. — ط مد ظله

The phrase refers to ‘those meanings’: the soul gathers together the meanings that make a thing what it is. It does not mean that the soul gives those meanings their very foundation. A feature that distinguishes one kind within a wider kind does not, simply by doing so, create the wider kind. The identity of a thing comes from its form and its final distinguishing feature. The features that came before are gathered into this last one, in a simpler and more complete way. As the final distinguishing feature, it gives the thing its definite identity. As the final form, it brings the earlier material into its completed state: it acts as the source of its fulfillment and as the end toward which it develops.

As the form proper to this kind of thing, it is also the source of the effects that belong to the kind. Because it contains the earlier levels in a fuller way, it can produce their effects as well. The earlier parts and features are therefore conditions that make this complete form possible, rather than separate sources of the finished thing's identity. This was explained in the First Journey.

One might object: if it is hard to understand what will is in general, it must also be hard to know any particular act of willing. After all, a particular instance is simply the general nature together with the features that make it this instance.

The answer is that identifying something as a particular example of a kind does not require us first to know that kind's complete definition. We can begin by knowing what the word points to; that simpler question comes before the harder questions about its nature.

There is also another answer. What we know directly from experience is that willing exists and occurs. What needs a definition is its nature. The same holds for the soul. We are directly aware of ourselves, although this awareness has degrees, yet it is hard to define the soul's nature. Thinkers even disagree over the broader kind to which it belongs: is it a substance, or something else?
If knowledge is a level of existence, defining it is difficult because existence itself is the most basic and familiar reality. — س قده
Some definitions confuse will with thought, judgment, desire, or inclination because these experiences often occur together.
The author's point is that knowledge does not always follow an event; some events follow from what is known. — س قده
Will and knowledge can differ because knowledge may be a more distant cause of an act while will is a nearer one. — س قده
Belief in benefit belongs to the knowing power, while will arises from the power that reaches toward action. They are not the same state.
“Cracking the fingers” means bending them until they make a sound. Even routine actions usually involve some desire: habit can be pleasant, and going against it unpleasant.
We may have a rational desire to take medicine while disliking its taste. The author argues that this means will and desire are not always identical. — س قده

When comparing will with existence, the author does not stop at existence. He also speaks here of goodness and, a few lines later, of pleasure, saying that existence is loved and enjoyed in every thing. This makes the comparison closer: it links acts of willing with what is wanted, and the levels of the two match one another.

Natural existence is not only something loved; in this account, it also loves, because even natural beings have a simple kind of awareness. So just as there is will in the sense of being wanted, there is also will in the sense of wanting. Desire and love spread through things both as their being objects of love and as their loving in return.
The author treats every level of existence as a kind of awareness, though ordinary speech calls only the clearest, least limited forms “knowledge.”
Even natural actions such as nourishment and growth can be understood as the soul acting through its powers and instruments. — س قده
The discussion concerns the powers that lead to action. Theoretical reason is not one of these; it is more complete and not directed toward a particular bodily act. — س قده

When the faculty of judgment uses these representations to join forms in its own way, they belong to that faculty. When it uses them to combine imagined forms, they are counted among the lower spiritual realm.

The comparison here makes another point. In the greater world, one outpouring passes through many levels on its way to lower things. At each level it takes on what is appropriate to that level, while remaining one outpouring. Likewise, will is one reality passing through the levels of the soul. As it descends, it becomes the tendency in the muscles to relax or contract, much as the natural impulse arises from powers that cause movement. It is one will running through all these levels, expressed differently at each one.

The author speaks of something “smokelike,” although the usual older medical term is the vapour-like spirit. He has already connected the two descriptions. The Qur'an, the Torah, and other texts speak of the heavens as smoke. This could be because the heavens are like a subtle, smokelike spirit in the body of the greater world; or because the heaven of the smaller world, the human being, is the vapour-like spirit.

The “layers” of this spirit refer to three kinds recognized in the old medical account. The brain has a spirit concerned with perception and the nerves are its channels. The heart has the vital spirit, carried through the arteries. The liver has the natural spirit, carried through the veins.

On this account, the spirit associated with the brain is finer and higher than that of the heart, and the heart's is finer than the liver's. Even within the brain, its rear part is said to be finer than its middle, and the middle finer than its front. The same ordering can be drawn within the front part. These are features of the historical theory, not present-day anatomy.

The author's elaborate reply may not be necessary. The objector has confused the meaning of a word with the reality to which it points. We can properly say that God knows everything, but not always that He wills everything in the same sense. This difference follows from what “knowledge” and “will” mean. It does not mean that God's knowledge and will are separate realities in Him.

The same point applies to His other attributes. We call Him living, knowing, powerful, hearing, and seeing. Yet we do not usually say that He hears what is seen or sees what is heard, because the words have different uses. “Life” is another example: in speaking of God, it does not point to something outside Him as knowledge does. We cannot freely exchange these words just because they all describe Him.

But if the mind looks beyond these different meanings to God's reality, each attribute belongs to His entire undivided being. He is powerful with the whole of His being, just as He is living with the whole of His being. In that sense He hears by what He sees and sees by what He hears. No part or side of His existence lacks a perfection found in another.
Evil, considered simply as evil, is a lack rather than a thing that exists. God does not will evil in itself, though some limited harms follow from greater goods. — ط
Another reading is that verses about God's approval concern what He approves in religious law, while this discussion concerns His will in creating. — ط مد ظله

The two replies answer different parts of the objection. The first denies the opponent's claim that God knows everything but does not will everything. It says that, just as His knowledge embraces all things, His will embraces everything that exists as good. The second reply addresses the claim that knowledge and will must be distinct realities: if God's knowledge is identical with His being, will must be an added attribute. Different meanings do not require different things. Hearing and sight, for example, can be distinguished from knowledge by what they concern without becoming separate additions to God's being. Knowledge concerns everything; sight concerns what can be seen. Similarly, will can be understood as knowledge of a thing insofar as it is good.

The first reply may be preferable because the second could seem to concede that some existing things fall outside God's will. But whatever exists has goodness insofar as it exists, and God's will embraces it on that account.
This points to the ordered way that many different things, including events that occur in time, can follow from one simple cause and one will. — س قده
Times may be alike in kind while still differing in their individual identity. That difference can explain why an event occurs at one time rather than another.
The point is that God wills the time itself to begin, not that He wills it at some earlier time. Otherwise we would have to ask when that earlier time began, and so on. — س قده
The world is treated as one ordered whole, like a single great human being, whose many individual beings are parts.

The point is not that God is compelled, as if someone or something passed a judgment requiring Him to act. Rather, His act follows necessarily from the way He acts: He makes it necessary, so it becomes necessary and exists.

The words “one who is required to act” are awkward here. Some theologians who reject necessity in God's actions nevertheless say that certain things are necessary for God, such as His doing what is best for His creatures. God is not compelled in that sense.

Perhaps, then, the author means an action imposed by some force, as the word “upon” suggests. That would be the kind of compulsion applied to natural processes, unlike an action that follows necessarily from God's own knowledge, power, and choice. Philosophers use the second sense. Because the words sound alike, critics sometimes accuse them of teaching the first. That accusation is unjust.
The author argues that God's action through His own will is the fullest kind of voluntary action. God's will is not an added state; it is His essence.
“Specific relations” means the ways God's attributes and names relate to particular kinds and individuals He creates. These relations do not divide His essence. — س قده

Without those particular relations, no specific creature would be distinguished from another. The author therefore says that God's action is necessary with reference to a particular will or relation. — س قده

This is a good explanation, but it does not yet answer the earlier objection. The meaning of will is not the same as knowledge of what is good or suitable. In our own experience, willing does not mean knowing. The state we call will goes together with knowledge, just as love, hatred, contentment, and anger may accompany knowledge, but their meanings are not identical with it. Removing the weaknesses of human willing does not suddenly turn its meaning into knowledge. For that reason, I think will should be understood from the action it produces, insofar as the action comes from God's irresistible power, or from the gathering of the causes that lead to an act, insofar as those causes depend upon Him.

We often call the preparation for an act ‘willing.’ If someone brings food, reaches for it, and puts it in his mouth, we say, ‘He wants to eat.’ Some have confused this kind of will, which is spoken of in relation to an act, with the very cause that brings existence into being. That is a serious error, for it would undermine the account of God's oneness. — ط مد ظله

The wording may be understood in another way. If the term is taken to mean an act in relation to something, it may refer to the one who acts or to what receives the action. The grammatical distinction matters here: being known is not the same as the thing known. The former is said literally of what is known; the latter can involve a figure of speech. This is a point about language, not yet the reconciliation sought here.

The commentator's concern is to preserve God's freedom from change. Knowledge, understood as God's being knowing, is eternal at every level, not something that begins in time. The same is true of will. The levels sometimes called providence, the Tablet, decree, and destiny are eternal insofar as they are God's knowledge.

A clearer reconciliation, in my view, is to distinguish two aspects of divine will. First, God's delight in His own reality belongs to His essence. Second, there is His love as expressed in action, through the giving of existence to all things. The latter is indicated by the saying that God created things through His will, and created the will itself. This is God's command, the word 'Be.' It also explains what some theologians mean when they say that God's willing is His command and His disapproval is His prohibition.

The first aspect is identical with God's essence. The second appears in His acts. Insofar as it is related to changing things, it can be described as coming about with them; insofar as it is related to God, it depends on His necessary and eternal being. It is like a meaning that exists only through its relation to something else. The will expressed in action is the appearance of the eternal will, not something separate from it.
Practical reason is the human power that judges what should be done. It differs from theoretical reason, which seeks knowledge, and from the animal powers of appetite and anger.
Desire arises from a sense of both having something and lacking it: the desired thing is present in thought but not yet possessed. — س قده
The report's phrase “what follows” refers to the action that follows our inner resolve. The action is not itself the will. — س قده
“Hollow” can suggest either a being that is made of parts or one that works through parts and powers.
